clue.text: Grace out for a century

parts.note: read as a lovely, graceful girl knocked out cold for a hundred years, the heroine of the fairy tale

explanation.surface: A cricketer named Grace is dismissed after scoring a hundred.
explanation.walkthrough: W. G. Grace was England's most famous Victorian cricketer, and a century is a hundred runs, so the surface is a batsman out on a hundred. Read again, grace is beauty and 'out' is unconscious for a hundred years.
explanation.definitionFit: The fairy-tale princess slept for a hundred years, so she is grace (loveliness) knocked out for a century.

clue.text: Rising American chap, so sweet !

indicators.note: in a down entry rising means the word is read from the bottom up, that is backwards

parts.note: Gary is a man's name, standing for a chap

explanation.surface: An American man who comes up in the world is so very sweet.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry 'Rising' reads its piece from the bottom up, so the abbreviation for American is turned; the chap is simply a man's first name.
explanation.definitionFit: Something full of sugar tastes very sweet, cloyingly so.

clue.text: Robin Hood's Bay is not, though in a this part of Yorks.

annotationWithheld.why: Robin Hood's Bay is not, though in a this part of Yorks. (6) -- the scan also reads 'in a this', which looks garbled; with no reprint, no parse ties 'though in a this part of Yorks.' to the answer
annotationWithheld.clue: Robin Hood's Bay is not, though in a this part of Yorks.

clue.text: Dance tempo for leisure hours?

parts.note: a pas is a step or dance in ballet
tempo in music means time

explanation.surface: Asking whether a dance rhythm suits one's free time.
explanation.walkthrough: PAS is the French ballet word for a dance step, as in pas de deux.
explanation.definitionFit: A hobby is something to fill leisure hours, a way of passing spare time.

clue.text: The Count is so unfeeling at first

indicators.note: only the opening part of the word is used, the rest of it is cut away

parts.note: a count or total is a number

explanation.surface: An aristocratic Count is described as cold and insensitive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Count' looks like a nobleman but is a number, a total; 'at first' keeps its first four letters and drops ER.
explanation.definitionFit: Without sensation, the way a frozen limb has no feeling.

clue.text: See 1
Cost of keeping swans in a river

indicators.note: one thing keeping another holds it within, so the swans go inside the river

parts.note: the Exe is a river in Devon
pens are female swans

explanation.surface: What it costs to keep swans on a river.
explanation.walkthrough: A pen is a female swan, a fact solvers often meet only in crosswords; the river is in Devon, south-west England. 'Keeping' sets the swans within the river.
explanation.definitionFit: An outlay or charge is a cost.

clue.text: Moving fluidly for a low pass

definitions.text: Moving fluidly for a low pass

parts.words: Moving fluidly for a low pass
parts.note: read as a ship moving through water, and also as a route or passage beneath something, a way going low

explanation.surface: Gliding smoothly to make a pass at ground level.
explanation.walkthrough: A ship that is moving through the water is said to be under way; split, the words describe a low passage, a route beneath.
explanation.definitionFit: A vessel making headway through water is said to be in motion, and the two words split describe a route that passes beneath.

clue.text: Copperfield was in the cart at the prospect of this

definitions.text: Copperfield was in the cart at the prospect of this

parts.words: Copperfield was in the cart at the prospect of this
parts.note: David Copperfield rode in the carrier Barkis's cart when he went to visit Peggotty's family at this Norfolk seaside town

explanation.surface: A boy in trouble on hearing where he is being sent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the cart' is British slang for in trouble, but in Dickens's novel young David rides in Barkis's cart for a stay in this Norfolk port with the Peggottys.
explanation.definitionFit: In Dickens the young hero is sent by carrier's cart to Peggotty's boat-house on the Norfolk coast.

clue.text: Hair-raising perhaps, that is to say made some grow

indicators.note: the phrase signals that the following words are to be spoken, giving a word that sounds like them

parts.note: if you made some grow, you grew some

explanation.surface: A tonic described as hair-raising because it made some hair grow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hair-raising' points at a hair restorer; in fact it is the definition, meaning horrifying.
explanation.definitionFit: Something horrifying makes the hair stand on end, so a grisly sight is hair-raising.

clue.text: An example to one who would rise at the seventh attempt

definitions.text: An example to one who would rise at the seventh attempt

parts.words: An example to one who would rise at the seventh attempt
parts.note: recalls the legend of Robert the Bruce in a cave, inspired by a creature that tried six times to climb its thread and succeeded on the seventh

explanation.surface: A model of perseverance for someone determined to succeed after repeated failures.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert the Bruce, the Scottish king, is said to have watched a web-spinner fail six times and succeed at the seventh, and so took heart to rise against the English again.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Bruce legend a web-spinning creature, by climbing on its seventh try, set the king an example of persistence.

clue.text: Lets bring them in

parts.note: read lets as nouns, properties leased to tenants, which bring in money paid by the occupants

explanation.surface: Someone urging that a group be admitted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lets' looks like 'let's' (let us), but it is the noun: a let is a property leased out, which earns its owner payments.
explanation.definitionFit: Leases bring in sums paid by tenants, the money a landlord earns from letting.

clue.text: That's too bad-hurried to the police

parts.note: hurried means ran
CID is the Criminal Investigation Department, the detective branch of British police

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims at bad news and rushes off to report it to the police.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That's too bad' reads as a sympathetic exclamation, but it defines food that has gone off, too far gone to eat.
explanation.definitionFit: Butter or fat that is spoiled and foul-smelling is gone off, far too bad to eat.

clue.text: Ointment Androcles might have used, given with love by an old master

parts.note: Androcles drew a thorn from a lion's paw; LEO (the lion) plus NARD (a fragrant ointment) is lion-ointment
love is zero in tennis scoring, the letter O

explanation.surface: An ointment, the sort Androcles could have used on the lion, is presented lovingly by a great painter.
explanation.walkthrough: In the fable Androcles pulled a thorn from a lion's paw, so his ointment would be 'Leo nard', a balm for the lion; NARD is spikenard, an aromatic ointment.
explanation.definitionFit: Da Vinci, the Renaissance painter, is one of the Old Masters, the great European artists before about 1800.

clue.text: Beamed by satellite

parts.note: read as lit up by the light of Earth's natural satellite at night

explanation.surface: A broadcast transmitted from orbit.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a satellite broadcast; the satellite is Earth's own, and 'beamed' means shone upon.
explanation.definitionFit: Shone upon by Earth's only natural satellite, as a night landscape is.

clue.text: Lubber's place at board as aboard ?

definitions.text: Lubber's place at board as aboard ?

parts.words: Lubber's place at board as aboard
parts.note: a clumsy landsman seated at table is placed in the humble lower half, and aboard ship he ranks beneath the old salts

explanation.surface: Where a clumsy seaman sits at table, both ashore and on board ship.
explanation.walkthrough: At old banquets the salt cellar stood mid-table and lesser guests sat beyond it; a lubber is an awkward novice sailor, beneath the experienced 'salts' in rank.
explanation.definitionFit: Lowly diners sat on the far side of the salt cellar, and a novice sailor ranks under the seasoned hands.

clue.text: Rebuffer of the Roman type?

parts.note: read as a short upturned feature of the face, the opposite kind to the high-bridged Roman, whose first word means rebuff

explanation.surface: A person who snubs anything in Roman lettering.
explanation.walkthrough: A Roman nose is large and hooked; the opposite type is short and turned up. To snub is to rebuff, so the feature 'rebuffs' the Roman one.
explanation.definitionFit: A short turned-up nose is the opposite shape to a hooked aquiline one, and to snub is to rebuff.

clue.text: Emphatic even to exasperation

parts.note: read as using strong language, oaths and curses, as people do when exasperated

explanation.surface: Insisting on a point so hard that it annoys.
explanation.walkthrough: Oaths are the most emphatic words, and people resort to them when exasperated.
explanation.definitionFit: Cursing and using oaths is the most forceful speech, the kind exasperation produces.

clue.text: Dog discovered by Cabot

definitions.meaning: a large, strong, water-loving breed of working dog
John Cabot reached this North Atlantic island in 1497, land newly found

explanation.surface: A hound that the explorer Cabot came across.
explanation.definitionFit: The big shaggy dog breed takes its name from the island, which the Venetian explorer Cabot sighted as new territory for England.

clue.text: Eye say !

definitions.meaning: to eye is to watch or look at
to say or remark, as in passing a comment

explanation.surface: A brief exclamation about an eye.
explanation.definitionFit: To watch closely and to remark both fit: one may watch a bird or remark that it is cold.

clue.text: Run late, shunting, there being no siding

indicators.note: shunting moves railway wagons about, so the letters of the two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A train runs late because of shunting, as there is no siding to pull into.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Siding' looks like railway track, but here it means taking a side. 'Shunting' rearranges RUN LATE.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking no side in a dispute is impartial, unaligned.

clue.text: Before noon father could be quite shocking !

parts.note: am, ante meridiem, means before noon
pere is French for father

explanation.surface: A father's behaviour before midday could be quite scandalous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shocking' suggests scandal, but the definition is electrical: the unit of current, which in quantity gives a shock.
explanation.definitionFit: The unit of electric current measures what delivers an electric shock, so a lot of it is shocking.

clue.text: Is uppish in consequence

definitions.meaning: comes about as a result, follows from something

explanation.surface: Someone becomes arrogant as a result.
explanation.definitionFit: To get up and to result from something share the word, as a problem may spring from neglect.

clue.text: One is on guard

parts.note: read as a tall fur cap worn by soldiers of the Guards regiments on sentry duty

explanation.surface: A sentry standing watch.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a sentry; the thing 'on guard' is the tall black fur hat on the guardsman's head outside Buckingham Palace.
explanation.definitionFit: The tall black fur cap of the British Foot Guards is worn on ceremonial guard duty.

clue.text: What' more suitable for the odd drink ?

definitions.text: What' more suitable for the odd drink ?

parts.words: What' more suitable for the odd drink
parts.note: read 'more suitable for the odd' as 'odder', the comparative of rum meaning strange, and the whole as a large glass for a drink

explanation.surface: Asking which vessel suits an occasional tipple better.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rum' is British slang for odd, so its comparative means 'more odd'; the word is also a large drinking goblet, a vessel for the odd drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A large stemmed drinking glass is a goblet for a drink, and the word is also the comparative of rum, meaning stranger.

clue.text: Scion shot on the green ?

definitions.meaning: a descendant, as in a ... off the old block
a short lofted golf stroke played near the putting area

explanation.surface: A young heir is shot on the village green.
explanation.definitionFit: A child resembling a parent is a chip off the old block, and a golfer's lofted short stroke onto the putting surface shares the name.

clue.text: Get them out of bed and get weaving !

definitions.text: Get them out of bed and get weaving !

parts.words: Get them out of bed and get weaving
parts.note: read the bed as a riverside plot where willows grow, and weaving as basketwork made from their cut stems

explanation.surface: A command to rouse the lazy and get busy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get weaving' is British slang for get a move on; here it is literal, because these willow rods are cut from their beds and woven into baskets.
explanation.definitionFit: Basket willows are grown in beds by water and their flexible rods are woven into wickerwork.

clue.text: Dishes of horseflesh

definitions.meaning: war horses ridden by knights or cavalry, collectively horseflesh

explanation.surface: Plates of horse meat on the menu.
explanation.definitionFit: A large flat platter and a cavalryman's mount share the word, so both plates and horses fit.

clue.text: Falsified age allowed to keep a bird young

indicators.note: a falsified thing is altered or doctored, so the letters of age are rearranged

parts.note: allowed means let

explanation.surface: Someone lied about their age so as to be allowed to keep a bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Falsified' rearranges AGE into EAG, which is followed by LET; 'to keep' is a link here.
explanation.definitionFit: A young eagle is a bird young, the chick of a raptor.

clue.text: The weird sisters at scrabble ?

parts.note: read the witches of Macbeth, who cast spells, as players of the word game who put words together

explanation.surface: Macbeth's three witches playing a board game.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'weird sisters' are the three witches in Shakespeare's Macbeth; they make spells, and at Scrabble every player spells out words.
explanation.definitionFit: Witches cast spells, and anyone forming words at Scrabble spells too, so both are people who spell.
